thread.title: Apple's share buyback is a smarter use of its cash than these 4 other options

author: morningstar.com
title: Apple's share buyback is a smarter use of its cash than these 4 other options
text:
By Gary Smith
If you like dividends, you will love share buybacks
When Apple announced that it would repurchase $100 billion worth of its stock (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/how-many-billions-is-apple-about-to-promise-its-investors-2018-05-01), investors cheered and pundits jeered. An economics professor at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell, who reportedly studies stock buybacks proclaimed that "it's nothing but a manipulation of the stock market."
Hogwash. It is almost impossible to manipulate--in any meaningful sense of the word--stocks that are as heavily traded as Apple(AAPL), and Apple's buyback is nothing more than a sensible way of distributing part of the company's earnings to Apple's owners, its shareholders.
Apple's stock price did increase after the buyback was announced but it wasn't because of some nefarious market manipulation. Investors liked Apple's second-quarter results; investors loved Warren Buffett's announcement that Berkshire Hathaway (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-adds-30-points-to-dow-after-report-that-buffett-bought-75-million-shares-2018-05-04)(BRKA) (BRKA) had purchased 75 million shares of Apple before the buyback was announced; and investors liked the fact that Apple was doing something smart with its cash.
If we want to think seriously about buybacks, instead of chanting political slogans and smears, let's consider what Apple might plausibly do with $100 billion in cash.
Hold on to it
There is a substantial opportunity cost to holding on to cash, or investing it in Treasury bills paying a modest interest rate. If Apple's shareholders can earn a 10% return on their investments and Apple has $100 billion invested in Treasury bills paying 2%, the opportunity cost is 8%, or $8 billion a year. The economic value added is negative $8 billion a year, which means Apple is destroying value instead of creating value.
It is better to deploy cash than to hoard it.
Pay off debt
Apple has more than $100 billion in debt, so it could the $100 billion of cash to pay off some of its borrowings. Although it superficially seems imprudent, U.S. tax laws reward companies that have (modest amounts of) debt. As with other corporations, Apple's debt is a tax shield because, unlike dividends, the interest Apple pays on its debt is tax-deductible. A company pays less in taxes if it is financed partly by debt instead of entirely by equity. The less that is paid in taxes, the more cash is available for bondholders and stockholders.
Admittedly, debt isn't a blessing if a firm goes bankrupt and lawyers charging $1,000 an hour have to sort out the mess, but Apple's debt is conservative and it increases its free cash flow.
Fund expansion
Apple could use its cash to hire more people, but hiring people for the sake of hiring people is a pretty bad business plan. Corporations are owned by their shareholders and should act in their best interests. Hiring more people and growing the firm only benefits shareholders if the company can earn a return on its investment that is greater than the return that the firm's shareholders can earn on their own. Otherwise, the firm is throwing away its shareholders' money, destroying value instead of adding value.
When Apple does find attractive opportunities to add value in the future, it won't have to worry about how to pay for them. Apple is a money machine that generates plenty of cash.
Pay dividends
If a company has more cash than it needs for new investments, it should give the cash to its shareholders--either through dividends or share repurchases--and let them do better. Apple, like most companies, pays dividends. However, shareholders have to pay taxes on their dividends, which bring us to buybacks, a better way to give cash to stockholders.
Repurchase shares
For firms that want to disburse some of their profits to shareholders, share repurchases can be better than dividends--and that is how we should think of stock buybacks, as a disguised dividend.
Instead of giving $100 billion to shareholders and calling it a dividend, Apple is giving $100 billion to shareholders and calling it a buyback. Either way, the value of Apple after it gives $100 billion to its shareholders is exactly the same--the same assets, the same products, the same customers whether it is a dividend or a buyback-- so the aggregate value of its stock should be the same, too. The only real difference is that the taxes shareholders have to pay on the $100 billion they receive depends on whether it is called a dividend or a buyback.
Unfortunately, there is a lot of misinformation about buybacks. Legendary fund manager Peter Lynch once argued that "if a company buys back half its shares and its overall earnings stay the same, the earnings per share have just doubled." The obvious flaw is that the firm may have to liquidate half its assets to buy back half its stock. How can earnings stay the same if the firm sheds half its assets?
A New York Times columnist made a similarly misleading argument about Apple's buyback when he wrote that buybacks "reliably lift stock prices by limiting the supply of shares for sale." Not true. The intrinsic value of a company's stock depend on how profitable a company is, not the supply of shares; so the real question is how buybacks affect a company's profits. If a firm liquidates half its assets in order to cut the supply of shares in half, then its assets per share are unchanged and there is no reason for the reduced supply of shares to increase the value of each share.
The real value of a buyback comes from the disbursement of idle cash, not from a change in the number of shares.
Read:Warren Buffett applauds Apple's share buybacks (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/warren-buffett-applauds-apples-share-buybacks-2018-05-05)
Let's ignore taxes for a moment and work through a simple example. A company has 20 million shares outstanding, each valued at $20 (an aggregate market value of $400 million). This firm has $20 million in cash to distribute to its shareholders. One alternative is to pay a $1 dividend per share; another is to buy back 1 million shares at $20 apiece. This table shows the consequences. Either way, the $20 million payout reduces the firm's aggregate value from $400 million to $380 million.
Initial position After $1 dividend After repurchasing 1 million shares Shares (in millions) 20 20 19 Price per share $20 $19 $20 Firm's total value (in millions) $400 $380 $380
If the firm pays a $1 dividend, each share is worth $1 less, since $380 million divided among 20 million shares is $19. The shareholders are no better or worse off since they started with $400 million in stock and now they have $20 million in cash and $380 million in stock.
If, instead, the firm repurchases shares, the number of shares declines by 1 million, and $380 million aggregate value divided among 19 million shares makes each share worth $20. No one is better or worse off. Those who sell their shares get $20 in cash for their stock; those who don't sell continue to have stock worth $20 a share.
Dividends and buybacks are alternative ways of giving a firm's shareholders some of the profits that the firm earns on their behalf. The crucial difference between dividends and buybacks is the tax consequences for shareholders, and this gives buybacks a clear advantage over dividends.
When a company pays dividends, all shareholders pay taxes, and they pay taxes on all the cash they receive. When a company repurchases stock, shareholders don't have to sell, and those who do sell only pay taxes on their capital gains. That may not be all of them. Some may have no capital gains and pay no taxes; others may have tax losses and receive a tax credit. The bottom line is that with buybacks, shareholders have a choice: to sell or not. Those who do sell don't have to pay as much in taxes as they would if the firm had disbursed the cash as dividends. Win-win.
The conclusion is simple and has nothing to do with market manipulation. Except for the benefits from avoiding taxes on dividends, a stock buyback is equivalent to paying dividends--a dividend in disguise. If you like dividends, you will love repurchases.
Apple did its shareholders a huge favor when it reduced their tax obligations by making part of its cash distribution a buyback instead of dividends.
Gary Smith (http://garysmithn.com/index.html) is the Fletcher Jones Professor of Economics at Pomona College and author of "Money Machine: The Surprisingly Simple Power of Value Investing (https://www.amazon.com/Money-Machine-Surprisingly-Simple-Investing/dp/0814438563)."
-Gary Smith; 1355ET
